name: The Caucasian Elm That Was Cut Back to Save It

location.address: Giardino dei Semplici, Via Pier Antonio Micheli 3, 50121 Firenze

story: In the 1980s this tree lost roughly two thirds of its height in a single operation, and it is still on the national register. The garden planted a Caucasian elm here in 1827 and it grew the way the species does, slowly, into a trunk now close to six metres around. Then a fungal outbreak arrived, named in one register as Dutch elm disease, and the answer was surgery rather than a saw at the base. The branches came off hard, and what stands today is a fluted grey column carrying a crown regrown out of the cuts. The national register still lists this tree at thirty metres tall. The 2021 field survey measured ten. Both numbers are honest, they simply belong to different decades, and the difference between them is the operation. Zelkova carpinifolia is not an elm, whatever everyone calls it. It is a close cousin from a small range in the Caucasus and along the southern shore of the Caspian, and it is planted across Europe precisely because it shrugs off the disease that emptied the continent of its elms, which is worth thinking about while standing in front of one that needed cutting back anyway. The trunk is the thing to look at: buttressed, silver, and wildly out of proportion to everything above it.
access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)
notes: MASAF 06/D612/FI/09. Three sources: the garden's own monumental-trees page (planted first half of the 1800s, heavily pruned in the 1980s against a fungal disease), RAMI 6488 (planted 1827, survey 14 Oct 2021, girth 5.75 m, height 10.00 m, past crown reduction for Dutch elm disease, GPS 43.778827/11.261576), and MASAF (girth 610 cm, height 30.0 m). REGISTER TRAP: MASAF's 30 m height predates the pruning and must never be quoted as current; the story uses the 2021 figure and explains the gap. Girth differs between sources (610 vs 575 cm) because they measure at different heights, so the story says 'close to six metres' rather than picking one. Both registers also use the older synonym Zelkova crenata. Alive, health surveyed 2021, inside the ticketed garden. No superlative claimed, so no conflict with flo_003's 'widest trunk in the city' (670 cm).

name: The Zelkova Somebody Keeps Measuring

location.address: Giardino dei Semplici, Via Pier Antonio Micheli 3, 50121 Firenze

story: Somebody has put a tape around this trunk three times in forty years: 3.30 metres in 1980, 3.89 in 2001, 4.40 in 2021. Very few trees anywhere carry that kind of paper trail, and it means you can watch this one grow at roughly two and a half centimetres of girth a year without waiting around for it. The garden planted it in 1891 and credits it with the widest crown in the whole collection, which in a place this old is a real claim. Zelkova serrata comes from Japan, Korea and eastern China, where it is the keyaki, the timber used for temple pillars and the bodies of taiko drums, and it is the species most often trained as a broom-form bonsai because the branching is naturally so even. At full size the same habit produces a vase: a short trunk dividing into a fan of near-equal limbs. The bark is the detail to look for. It flakes off in small rounded plates and leaves orange patches underneath, so the trunk reads as a mosaic rather than a texture, and it is the fastest way to pick this tree out from the path. In autumn the leaves turn orange and rust before they drop.
access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)
notes: MASAF 04/D612/FI/09 (girth 453 cm, height 25.0 m). AGE CONFLICT, resolved in favour of the garden: sma.unifi.it says planted 1891, RAMI 6499 credits it to Ottaviano Targioni Tozzetti in the early 1800s and estimates over 200 years, and a Tuscany survey says 120 years. RAMI's attribution is 86 years off the garden's own record and is almost certainly bleed-over from the cork oak, which Targioni Tozzetti really did plant in 1805. The garden's record is used and RAMI's date is not repeated anywhere in the story. RAMI's 2021 survey (girth 4.40 m at 130 cm, height 26.0 m, health 'sufficiente') corroborates MASAF's measurements and supplies the 1980/2001/2021 growth series. SUPERLATIVE CHECK: the live flo_002 story claims the cork oak has 'one of the widest, most theatrical crowns in the Giardino dei Semplici'. The garden's own page gives the widest crown to this zelkova. The claim here is attributed to the garden rather than asserted; whoever merges should decide which of the two entries keeps it. PHOTO: downloaded and viewed at 960 px. The tree is the subject and the mosaic bark is exactly as described, but the framing is tighter than the Cadiz standard wants and the full crown is not readable, so it stays found_needs_check rather than approved.

best_time.label: October and November, when the leaves turn orange and rust

name: The Flag-Crowned Pine
age_estimate: over 130 years, in the garden since the late 1800s

location.address: Giardino dei Semplici, Via Pier Antonio Micheli 3, 50121 Firenze

story: The garden keeps this pine under constant watch, and says so in print, because its crown has grown into a flag. Almost all the weight sits on one side of a long bare trunk thirty-three metres up, which is what happens when a tree spends a century reaching for the only gap in a crowded collection, and it is also the shape most likely to fail in a storm. Publishing that about a tree you are proud of is unusually frank. The pine has been in the collection since the late 1800s and took up its present position in 1922. It is the Turkish pine, though Italian sources call it pino bruzio after Calabria, and botanists have argued for a century over whether it is a species in its own right or a subspecies of the Aleppo pine; the national register still files it under Pinus halepensis. It comes from the eastern Mediterranean, from Turkey and Cyprus and the Levant, where it is the pine that colonises burnt ground first and where resin was tapped from it for centuries. Its needles are longer and darker than the Aleppo pine's, and its cones sit almost stalkless against the branch, pointing forwards. Stand back towards the garden wall to take in the whole of it.
access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)
notes: MASAF 03/D612/FI/09 (girth 382 cm, height 33.5 m). Second source is the garden's own page (present from the late 1800s, moved to its current position in 1922, flag-shaped crown needing constant monitoring); the Regione Toscana monumental census independently gives 384 cm and 33.4 m, matching MASAF to within 2 cm and 10 cm. No source gives a planting year, so the age is published as a floor rather than a figure, and 1922 is described as a repositioning because that is exactly what the source says. SUPERLATIVE CHECK: an earlier draft called this the tallest tree in the garden. It is not. MASAF gives the cork oak (flo_002) 35.0 m against this tree's 33.5 m, so the claim was removed before shipping. Species naming: MASAF files it as Pinus halepensis var. brutia and the garden as Pinus halepensis subsp. brutia; published under the canonical Pinus brutia and deliberately kept separate from the three existing 'Aleppo Pine (Pinus halepensis)' entries on the site, because it is a different taxon. PHOTO: downloaded and viewed at 960 px. Whole tree in daylight against sky, trunk and flag crown both readable, centre band holds the tree so it survives the wide card crop. Approved.

name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Semplici
age_estimate: at least 146 years, on the garden's books from 1880

location.address: Giardino dei Semplici, Via Pier Antonio Micheli 3, 50121 Firenze

story: The Himalayan cedar only reached Europe in 1822, and this one was on the garden's books by 1880, which makes it an early adopter of a tree that half the continent would go on to plant in every park it built. It has had at least 146 years to make the case: four and a fifth metres round, twenty-eight metres up, with the drooping branch tips that separate a deodar from the stiffer cedars of Lebanon and the Atlas. The leading shoot nods over instead of standing straight and the outer branches hang in soft grey-green curtains, which is the quickest way to tell the three cedars apart from thirty metres off, and worth knowing here because a cedar of Lebanon grows across the river at the Bobolino. In its own range, from Afghanistan through Kashmir to western Nepal, this species reaches sixty metres on mountainsides at two thousand metres, and its wood resists rot well enough that Himalayan temples were built from it. Deodar comes from devadaru, the Sanskrit for timber of the gods. The garden acquired it during the decades when European collections competed for Himalayan and Mexican material, the same appetite that brought the Montezuma cypress here four years later. It is evergreen, so it looks much the same whenever you come, which is a reason to go rather than a reason to wait.
access: Paid entry (Orto Botanico ticket, standard museum admission)
transport: 5 min walk from Piazza San Marco (T2 tram stop)
notes: MASAF 07/D612/FI/09 (girth 418 cm, height 28.0 m). Second source is the garden's own page, which records the tree in the collection from 1880 and describes its imposing dimensions and drooping branches. 1880 is a first-record date, not a planting date, so the age is published as a floor with a wide upper bound. SPECIES NAMING, needs a human decision: this uses 'Himalayan Cedar (Cedrus deodara)', the majority form across the site (5 entries against 3 for 'Deodar Cedar'), but the live flo_008 in this same city file says 'Deodar Cedar (Cedrus deodara)'. As it stands the two Florence cedars would land on different species pages, which hard rule 9 exists to prevent. Renaming flo_008 is a one-line fix to the live file and was deliberately not made here. PHOTO GAP IS DELIBERATE: a CC BY-SA 3.0 Commons image exists (File:Cedrus deodara 01 by Line1.jpg, same photographer and day as the other two garden photos) and was downloaded and viewed at 960 px. It is a dark, backlit shot up into the crown in which the tree cannot be read at all and the imposing dimensions are invisible. It fails the Cadiz standard on exposure and on crown-and-trunk readability, so it was rejected. An honest gap beats a bad photo.

name: The Tree of the Newlyweds

location.address: Giardino del Bobolino, Viale Machiavelli, 50125 Firenze

story: Two enormous branches rise parallel to the trunk like a pair of horns, and Florence has been making the obvious joke for generations: locals know this tree as l'albero dei cornuti, the tree of the cuckolds. Newlyweds pose in front of it anyway, in such numbers that it picked up a politer second name, l'albero degli sposi, and both names are still in use. It is an incense cedar, native to the mountains of Oregon and California, and its trunk is five and a half metres around at chest height, which for the species in Europe is close to extraordinary. It stands to the left of the central flowerbed in the Giardino del Bobolino, the middle section of the English-style garden Giuseppe Poggi built along the Viale dei Colli between 1865 and 1877, when Florence was briefly the capital of Italy and Poggi was rebuilding its hillsides. Crush a fallen leaf spray and it smells sharply resinous, which is where the name comes from. A severe storm in the winter of 1985 damaged the trunk badly and it recovered. The city gave it formal protection in 2020. The cedar of Lebanon on this page stands a few steps away, so the two are one stop, not two.
transport: 15 min walk from Porta Romana, along Viale Machiavelli
notes: MASAF 11/D612/FI/09. Chosen specifically to thicken an existing walk: it stands about 45 m from the live flo_007 (Cedar of the Bobolino) and roughly 600 m from flo_008, so it costs a visitor nothing to add. RAMI 6484 gives girth 5.40 m at 130 cm, height 15.00 m, health 'good', accessibility 'accessible', survey 14 Oct 2021, GPS 43.757674/11.248871, and records both nicknames. The comune's own parks page independently confirms the tree ('cedro dell'incenso', on the left of the central bed) and dates the garden to Poggi, 1865-1877. FLAGGED FOR AGE: no source gives this tree an age. RAMI records 'not available'. The range published here is inferred from the garden's construction dates and is stated as undocumented in the age_estimate field, matching how the live flo_007 and flo_008 handle the same problem. A figure of 1850 plus or minus 20 circulates on monumentaltrees.com; per hard rule 1 that was used only to check that the inference is not absurd, and it is not cited or relied on. Species naming: no Calocedrus entry exists elsewhere on the site, so 'Incense Cedar' is set as the canonical form here in preference to the national 'California Incense-cedar'.
